title: How to Save Money: Restore, Don't Replace Your Deck
metaTitle: Restore vs Replace a Deck: Save Thousands | Kitchener

body.text: Every spring in Kitchener-Waterloo, homeowners walk out to a deck that has gone grey over the winter, feels rough underfoot and looks tired next to the rest of the yard. The instinct is almost always the same: this thing needs to be torn out and rebuilt. In the vast majority of cases, that instinct is wrong. A weathered deck is usually a wood surface that has lost its protective finish, not a structure that has failed. Restoring it can bring the same deck back to a near-new appearance for a small fraction of what a rebuild costs, and it is the approach Restore My Deck recommends unless an inspection turns up a genuine structural problem.
The real cost gap between replacement and restoration

A full deck replacement in Southwestern Ontario, including demolition, new framing, decking material, railings and permits where required, typically runs $15,000 to $40,000 depending on size, material choice and complexity. Composite decking and elaborate multi-level designs push costs toward the top of that range, while a simple pressure-treated rebuild sits closer to the bottom.

A professional deck restoration, by comparison, is priced very differently. Power washing and cleaning-only projects typically run $800 to $1,200 by area, while a full staining project including prep work usually falls between $950 and $1,350. Even an overdue deck that needs some board repairs alongside cleaning and staining generally lands under $2,500. That is a savings of 85 to 95 percent over replacement, for a result that, from ground level, most people cannot tell apart from new decking.
Why decks look worse than they actually are

The grey or silver colour that alarms most homeowners is UV damage to the surface wood fibres, not evidence of rot. Sunlight breaks down lignin, the compound that binds wood fibres together, and once that surface layer degrades the wood looks aged even though the boards underneath are perfectly sound. This is a cosmetic and protective problem, and it responds well to a proper clean, a light sand and a fresh coat of stain. The mistake many homeowners make is assuming that because the deck looks bad, it must be structurally compromised. In our experience inspecting decks across Kitchener, Waterloo, Cambridge and the surrounding area, that is rarely the case.

Restoration is almost always the right call when a deck meets a few basic conditions. First, the structural frame, ledger board and joists underneath the decking are still solid, with no significant rot or sagging. Second, the surface boards themselves are weathered, greyed or faded but not deeply rotted or soft to the touch. Third, the railings are intact and don't wobble significantly when pushed. And fourth, the deck is generally under 15 to 20 years old, although well-built older decks can sometimes qualify too.

Surface boards are grey or faded but not soft or spongy
Railings are stable and don't flex noticeably when pushed

body.text: Most decks that come across our schedule fall squarely into this category. Homeowners are often surprised at how much colour and texture returns once the deck has been properly cleaned, repaired where needed, sanded and stained. See /deck-restoration for how the full process comes together, and /5-signs-your-deck-needs-restoration for a more detailed breakdown of the warning signs worth checking before you call anyone.

There are situations where restoration genuinely will not solve the problem, and being upfront about them matters. If the joists or the ledger board connecting the deck to the house have rotted through, no amount of surface staining fixes that, because the structure itself is unsafe. Widespread soft, spongy boards across the whole deck, rather than one or two isolated spots, usually points to a moisture problem that has been progressing for years. And a deck that was undersized or poorly built to begin with, with inadequate footings or spacing, may not be worth investing further money into regardless of its surface condition.

If we find structural issues that require replacement during your inspection, we will tell you honestly rather than sell you a restoration that will not hold. In our experience, though, most decks in the Kitchener-Waterloo area are restorable.
What a professional restoration actually includes

A proper deck restoration is a four-step process, and skipping any one of them is what causes stain jobs to fail early. It starts with a deep clean using eco-friendly, plant-safe, VOC-compliant solutions that lift out mold, algae and the grey surface fibres that make weathered wood look dull. Depending on the wood type and condition, this is done through power washing, soft washing or a combination of both, since pressure-treated lumber and cedar respond differently to each method. See /pressure-washing-vs-soft-washing-deck for how we decide which approach a given deck needs.

Next comes repairs. Loose boards, popped fasteners and any genuinely rotted sections are addressed before anything else happens, because stain cannot fix a structural problem, it can only hide one temporarily. After repairs and a full drying period, the entire deck gets an 80-grit buff sand, which smooths the surface, removes any grain raised by the cleaning step and opens the wood pores so the stain can penetrate properly rather than sitting on top. Finally, we brush-apply a premium penetrating oil-based stain, typically Ready Seal or Penofin Verde, which soaks into the wood fibres rather than forming a surface film. That is what allows the finish to fade gracefully over the years instead of peeling. A final inspection closes out the job. Most restoration projects finish in about two days including drying time, with larger properties taking closer to three.
How long a restoration lasts, and what that means for your money

With a premium oil-based stain and proper prep work behind it, most decks go two to four years before they need a maintenance re-stain, and a full restoration every five to seven years keeps the deck looking sharp and extends its usable lifespan well beyond what an unmaintained deck would achieve. Staying on that cycle is, dollar for dollar, the most cost-effective way to protect a deck over its lifetime, since catching wear early always costs less than catching it late. A deck that gets restained on schedule rarely needs anything beyond a clean and a fresh coat. One that gets neglected for a decade may need board replacement or more extensive repair work layered on top of the standard process, which is a good reason not to let a stain job go too far past its expiry date. More on that timing in /how-often-should-you-restain-your-deck.

faq.q: How much does deck restoration cost compared to replacement?
faq.a: Replacement in Southwestern Ontario typically runs $15,000 to $40,000 depending on size and materials. A professional restoration, including cleaning, repairs and staining, usually falls between $950 and $2,500, a savings of roughly 85 to 95 percent.

faq.q: How do I know if my deck can be restored instead of replaced?
faq.a: If the frame and joists are structurally sound, the surface boards are weathered but not deeply rotted, the railings are stable, and the deck is generally under 15 to 20 years old, restoration is almost always the right call. A free inspection will confirm this for your specific deck.

faq.q: Does grey, weathered wood mean my deck is failing?
faq.a: No. Grey colouration is UV damage to the surface wood fibres, not evidence of rot or structural failure. It is a cosmetic and protective issue that responds well to professional cleaning, sanding and a fresh coat of oil-based stain.

faq.q: What does a professional deck restoration actually include?
faq.a: Four steps: a deep eco-friendly clean using power washing or soft washing depending on the wood, repairs to any loose or damaged boards, an 80-grit buff sand, and a brush-applied premium oil-based stain such as Ready Seal or Penofin Verde, finished with a final inspection.

faq.q: How long does a restoration take to complete?
faq.a: Most restoration projects are completed in about two days including drying time. Larger properties or those needing more extensive repairs typically take about three days.

faq.q: Will you ever tell me my deck actually needs replacing?
faq.a: Yes. We inspect every deck before quoting, and if we find rotted joists, a failing ledger board, or other structural issues that restoration cannot fix, we will tell you honestly rather than sell you a stain job that will not last.
